0.title: Why a Shepherd?
0.essay:
When the Bible wants to tell us how God cares for his people, it reaches again and again for one picture. Not a king on a throne, though God is King, but a man out on the hills with a flock, a stick in his hand and the sheep following him home.

The Bible’s favourite picture of care

The picture runs from the first family to the last book. Abel kept sheep. Jacob called God “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day” (Genesis 48:15). David, who had done the job, wrote the words most people know by heart: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). Then Jesus stood up in Jerusalem and said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). And in the last book of the Bible, the one who shepherds God’s people for ever is the Lamb.

The people who first heard these words knew sheep. Most of us do not, and the picture has gone a little soft, more greetings card than hillside. This study tries to bring it back into focus.

What this study does

We begin with real animals and real work: what sheep are actually like, and what a shepherd’s life was like in Bible lands and still is today. We will try to be accurate, and leave aside some popular claims that do not stand up. Then we will read Psalm 23 line by line with the shepherding behind it, hear the prophets’ anger at false shepherds and their promise of a true one, and come to Jesus, the good shepherd who became the Lamb. We end with what it means to live as his sheep, today and in the last valley.

The commentary notes on Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34 and John 10 go verse by verse; this study gathers the whole picture.

The chapters

What Sheep Are Like; The Shepherd’s Life; The LORD Is My Shepherd; False Shepherds and the Promised Shepherd; The Shepherd Who Became the Lamb; and Living as His Sheep.

For reflection

When you hear the words “The LORD is my shepherd”, what picture comes to mind? Where in your life right now do you most need a shepherd?

1.title: What Sheep Are Like
1.essay:
God could have compared us to lions, or eagles, or oak trees. He chose sheep. That is not an insult. It is an honest description, and it comes from someone who loves the animal he is describing.

The real animal

A sheep is a grazing animal and a prey animal. It has no claws, no fangs, no armour and no great speed. Its main defence is the flock. A sheep alone becomes distressed and calls out, and in danger the flock bunches together. When something frightens them, a dog, a sudden noise, a shadow across the path, sheep tend to panic and run, and a flock can scatter across a hillside in moments.

Sheep also wander, though not out of wickedness. A grazing sheep walks with its head down, moving from one mouthful to the next. It does not look up to see where the flock has gone. An hour later it lifts its head and finds itself alone, on the wrong side of a ridge or caught in a thorn bush. It simply followed the grass.

And they follow. Sheep follow the sheep in front of them, which usually keeps a flock together, but not always. In 2005 it was reported from eastern Turkey that hundreds of sheep went over a cliff after one jumped, while the shepherds were at breakfast. That is the flocking instinct with no shepherd to direct it.

A word about sermon illustrations

You may have heard that sheep are the most stupid animals on earth. That is not what the research shows. Scientists at Cambridge found that sheep could recognise the faces of around fifty other sheep and remember them for up to two years, and sheep recognise people too. Their problem is not a lack of brains. It is that they are made to live under care.

You may also have heard that a sheep that falls over on its back is helpless. Most sheep that lie down or roll get up again without any trouble. But a heavy ewe, especially one in full fleece or carrying lambs, can roll into a hollow and be unable to get her feet back under her. Shepherds call such a sheep cast. Gas builds up in her stomach, and in warm weather she can die within hours if no one finds her. So a good shepherd walks the field looking for her, and rolls her gently back onto her feet. It is a true and tender picture, if we do not stretch it.

Some illustrations should simply be dropped. There is no good evidence that shepherds in Bible lands broke the legs of wandering lambs to teach them to stay close. The Bible’s shepherd does the reverse: “I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16).

What Scripture means by calling us sheep

When the Bible calls us sheep, it means at least three things. First, we wander. “All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6). The psalmist prays, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant” (Psalm 119:176). Much of our straying is like the sheep’s: not one dramatic break, but head-down drift, one small mouthful after another, until we look up and find we are far from God. Yet Isaiah does not let us off: we have each turned “to his own way” (Isaiah 53:6). Our drift is real sin, not just bad luck.

Second, we are defenceless. Jesus saw the crowds, and “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). What moved him was not their stupidity but their exposure: worn out, and preyed on by leaders who did not care.

Third, we belong. “It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 100:3). Sheep are not wild animals. They are kept. God says to his people, “you are my sheep, human sheep of my pasture” (Ezekiel 34:31). He does not think less of us for being sheep. He made us, and he cares for us himself.

Dependence is not failure

Our culture prizes independence and hides its needs. But dependence is not a fault in a sheep. It is what a sheep is. And dependence on God is not a fault in us. It is the human condition, the way we were made from the beginning, long before sin. Sin did not make us dependent. Sin made us pretend we were not, and wander off to prove it.

The good news comes in the same verse as the bad. Peter writes, “For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). Being a sheep is not the problem. Being a sheep with no shepherd is.

An example

A retired nurse had spent her life caring for others and never once asked for help. After a fall she could not dress herself for weeks. She hated it. Then a friend read Psalm 100:3 with her, and she began to see that she had always been as dependent on God as she now was on her neighbours. She had only not noticed. Learning to say thank you to the people who helped her became, slowly, a way of learning to rest in the Shepherd.

For reflection

In what ways do you see yourself in the description of sheep: wandering, defenceless, or belonging? Where is your straying more like head-down drift than open rebellion? Why do you think Jesus responded to the crowds with compassion rather than contempt? What would it mean for you to accept your dependence on God rather than hide it?

2.title: The Shepherd’s Life
2.essay:
Shepherding in Bible lands was hard, lonely, outdoor work, with long walks for water, nights in the open, wild animals and thieves. God called many of his servants from this work, and he chose it as a picture of himself.

Water and grass in a dry land

Much of the land is green only for part of the year. The winter rains bring fresh grass to the hills, and by early summer much of it has burnt brown. A shepherd had to know where the grass lasted, which springs and wells did not fail, and where there was shade. Flocks moved with the seasons, often onto the stubble of harvested fields in summer. At wells the shepherds drew water into troughs for their animals, and several flocks might wait together until the stone was rolled back (Genesis 29:2–3). Flocks in Bible lands were often mixed, sheep with goats, which is why Jesus could speak of a shepherd who “separates the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32).

Leading, calling and counting

In the East the shepherd usually went in front of the flock and the sheep followed. Travellers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries often described a shepherd walking ahead and calling, and several told of a flock ignoring a stranger who tried the same call. Shepherds in Britain today often drive from behind with dogs, and that is real shepherding too. But the Bible’s picture is mostly the one who goes before: “he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice” (John 10:4).

A shepherd counted. Jeremiah speaks of a day when “flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them” (Jeremiah 33:13). The law of the tithe speaks of “every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman’s staff” (Leviticus 27:32). At evening the flock went one by one past him, and he knew if one was missing.

Tools and nights

The shepherd carried little: a rod, a short club for beating off animals and thieves; a staff, a longer stick for walking, guiding and reaching a sheep in trouble. A sling, and a bag for his food: David went out to Goliath with “his staff in his hand” and stones in “his shepherd’s pouch” (1 Samuel 17:40). Job speaks of “the dogs of my flock” (Job 30:1). At night the flock was kept in a fold, a pen of stones, sometimes topped with thorn branches, sometimes built against a cave (1 Samuel 24:3). Out in the hills, later travellers report, the shepherd might lie down across the gap in the wall, so that nothing went in or out except over him.

The dangers were real. In Bible times lions and bears lived in the land, as well as wolves, leopards and hyenas. David told Saul, “when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock, I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth” (1 Samuel 17:34–35). If an animal was killed, a hired shepherd could bring back what was left as evidence that he had not stolen it (Exodus 22:13). Amos uses that grim detail: “As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear” (Amos 3:12). Jacob summed up twenty years of the work: “by day the heat consumed me, and the cold by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes” (Genesis 31:40).

Shepherds in the Bible

Abel “was a keeper of sheep” (Genesis 4:2). Rachel first appears with her father’s flock, “for she was a shepherdess” (Genesis 29:9). Moses spent long years with Jethro’s sheep in the wilderness before God met him at the burning bush (Exodus 3:1). David was out “keeping the sheep” (1 Samuel 16:11) when Samuel came to anoint a king. Amos said, “the LORD took me from following the flock” (Amos 7:15).

Shepherds were not always honoured. Joseph warned his brothers that “every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians” (Genesis 46:34). Some Jewish writings from after the New Testament list herdsmen among trades thought untrustworthy, perhaps because flocks grazed on other people’s land. Scholars debate how far that attitude went in Jesus’ day, so we should not overstate it, but shepherds were not people of rank. And when God announced the birth of his Son, the first to hear were “shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night” (Luke 2:8).

Why God chose shepherds to lead

Ancient kings, such as Hammurabi of Babylon centuries before David, liked to call themselves shepherds. God filled the title with his own meaning. Moses asked God for a leader “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). Of David it says, “He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70), and “With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand” (Psalm 78:72).

A shepherd’s work trains the heart a leader needs: patience with the slow, attention to the weak, courage in danger, a life spent for others. God wanted leaders like that, because he is like that.

An example

A woman who grew up on a hill farm remembers lambing time. Her father barely slept for three weeks. He was out at two in the morning with a torch, checking ewes, and warming weak lambs by the kitchen stove. When she reads that the Lord “will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4), she thinks of her father, and then of how much greater God is.

For reflection

Which part of the shepherd’s life most surprises you? Why do you think God so often called shepherds to lead his people? What does it tell you about God that he announced his Son’s birth to shepherds first? Who has shepherded you with that kind of costly care?

3.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
3.essay:
David knew the job from the inside. In Psalm 23 he looks at it from the other side: what is it like to be a sheep with a shepherd who never fails? Each line rests on real work.

Long before David

David did not invent the picture. Jacob, an old man who had been a shepherd for decades, blessed his grandsons in the name of “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day” (Genesis 48:15). He also called God “the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel” (Genesis 49:24). Later Israel prayed, “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock” (Psalm 80:1). And Isaiah promised, “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). That last line is pure shepherding: a ewe heavy with lamb or nursing one cannot be hurried, and a good shepherd sets the pace by the slowest.

I shall not want

“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). The word my is bold: Israel knew God as the shepherd of the nation, but David says he is mine. As the commentary on this psalm notes, that is not a promise of everything he wants, but of everything a sheep needs, which is a better promise.

Green pastures and still waters

“He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters” (Psalm 23:2). In a dry land, green grass has to be found. Sheep, like cattle, graze and then lie down to chew the cud. A flock lying down in the heat of the day, unafraid, is a flock that has been fed and feels safe. That is why the bride in the Song asks her beloved where he will “make it lie down at noon” (Song of Songs 1:7).

Still waters are literally “waters of rest”. Sheep can drink from a stream, but a fast current or a steep bank is hard and risky for them, and a sheep soaked through in a heavy fleece is in trouble. So the shepherd looks for a quiet pool, or draws water into a trough.

He restores my soul

“He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (Psalm 23:3). The word restores means to bring back. The shepherd does it for the sheep that has wandered, and for the one too spent to go on. Anyone who has walked in the Judean wilderness has seen them: narrow tracks along the hillsides, worn by generations of flocks. The shepherd takes the one that gets home. And he does it for his own name’s sake, because a shepherd who loses his sheep is shamed.

The dark valley

“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me” (Psalm 23:4). The wilderness is cut by deep, narrow ravines. They can be the way to water and to new pasture, but they are dark, and they are where danger hides. A shepherd takes the flock through.

The rod and staff are the tools from the last chapter. The rod drives off the wolf. The staff guides and rescues. The Hebrew word for rod is the one used of the rod the sheep passed under to be counted (Ezekiel 20:37; in Leviticus 27:32 the ESV translates it “staff”). To a frightened sheep in a dark ravine, the shepherd’s stick says: he is here, he is armed, and he is counting.

The table and the oil

“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (Psalm 23:5). The plainest reading is that the picture moves from the field to a house, with God as a generous host; oil on the head was a host’s welcome (Luke 7:46). Yet a shepherd would hear something too. Olive oil was the ordinary salve for wounds (Isaiah 1:6), and shepherds have long used it on their sheep’s cuts and scratches, and in some places against biting flies. The God who welcomes us also tends our injuries.

Goodness and mercy

“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 23:6). The verb is strong, more like pursue. David had been chased by enemies; now God’s goodness and steadfast love are on his trail, and they will catch him. “And I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever” (Psalm 23:6). The sheep comes home, and stays.

If you would like more on the details of shepherding behind this psalm, W. Phillip Keller’s A Shepherd Looks at Psalm 23 is warm and much loved. It draws on his own sheep ranching in the twentieth century, so not every detail will match ancient Israel.

An example

A man in his fifties lost his job and spent a year looking for work. He prayed Psalm 23 most mornings, and says the line that held him was not the green pastures but “He leads me”. He could not see the path, but he could trust the one walking in front.

For reflection

Which line of Psalm 23 do you most need this week, and why? What is the difference between not wanting and having everything you want? What valley are you walking through, or have you walked through, and how was the Shepherd with you there? How does it change things that goodness and mercy are pursuing you?

4.title: False Shepherds and the Promised Shepherd
4.essay:
If God is the shepherd of his people, what happens when the human shepherds he appoints fail? The prophets answer with anger and with hope. God will judge the bad shepherds, and he will come and shepherd his flock himself.

Shepherds who fed themselves

Israel’s kings, priests and leaders were meant to be shepherds under God. Many were not. Jeremiah says, “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” (Jeremiah 23:1). Ezekiel says the same with a list that reads like a shepherd’s checklist turned upside down: “The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them” (Ezekiel 34:4).

Every item on that list is a real job on a real farm: extra feed for the weak, treatment for the sick, binding for the injured, fetching strays, searching for the lost, sometimes for hours. These shepherds did none of it. They took the wool and the meat and let the flock go. “So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd” (Ezekiel 34:5). The shepherds existed. They just did not shepherd.

Zechariah adds a darker picture, of a shepherd “who does not care for those being destroyed, or seek the young or heal the maimed or nourish the healthy, but devours the flesh of the fat ones” (Zechariah 11:16). A shepherd who eats the flock is the worst betrayal the trade can imagine.

I, I myself

Then comes one of the most moving promises in the Old Testament. “Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). God does not send another committee. He comes. “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down” (Ezekiel 34:15). And he does every job the bad shepherds left undone: “I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16).

Notice that he searches “on a day of clouds and thick darkness” (Ezekiel 34:12). A real shepherd knows that is when sheep get lost: in fog, in storm, when the flock cannot see. God does not wait for fine weather to look for his people.

My servant David

But in the same chapter God makes a second promise. “And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd” (Ezekiel 34:23). David had been dead for nearly four hundred years. This is a new David, a king from his line. Jeremiah says the same: God will raise up “for David a righteous Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5), whose name will be “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6).

So which is it? Will God shepherd his people himself, or will a son of David do it? The prophets hold both promises side by side without explaining how they fit. Micah adds that the ruler would come from Bethlehem, the shepherd town where David grew up (Micah 5:2), and “he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD” (Micah 5:4).

Strike the shepherd

Then Zechariah says something very strange. “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me … Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7). This shepherd is God’s own, a man who stands at God’s side. And the sword that strikes him is God’s sword.

In Ezekiel the bad shepherds are judged. In Zechariah the good shepherd is struck. Why would God strike his own shepherd? The Old Testament leaves the question hanging. The night before he died, Jesus picked it up. “You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered’” (Matthew 26:31). He was saying: I am that shepherd, and this is that night.

The stage is set

By the end of the Old Testament, then, the reader is waiting for someone who is both God himself come to seek his sheep, and David’s son set over them; who will be born in Bethlehem; and who will be struck by God’s own sword for the flock. Only one person has ever fitted that description. When Matthew tells of the wise men, he quotes Micah: “from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel” (Matthew 2:6). And when Jesus stood up in the temple and said “I am the good shepherd”, his hearers, steeped in Ezekiel, knew exactly what he was claiming.

An example

A young man left a church where the leader controlled everyone’s decisions and shamed anyone who questioned him. For a long time he could not read the word shepherd without flinching. Reading Ezekiel 34 helped him. He saw that God is angry at shepherds like that, and that the true Shepherd binds up the injured instead of using them. It was the start of trusting a church again, slowly, with careful friends beside him.

For reflection

Read Ezekiel 34:4 and 34:16 side by side. What does God promise to do that the bad shepherds failed to do? Why do you think God says “I, I myself”? How do the two promises of Ezekiel 34, God himself and a son of David, meet in Jesus? What does it mean that the shepherd in Zechariah 13:7 is struck by God’s own sword?

5.title: The Shepherd Who Became the Lamb
5.essay:
Every shepherd in Israel risked his life for his flock, and hoped to live. Jesus said something no shepherd had ever said: that he would save the flock by dying. Then the picture turns over: the shepherd becomes the lamb.

I am the good shepherd

In John 10 Jesus gathers up the whole shepherding world of his hearers. The fold with its single way in: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10:9). The shepherd who “calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3). The thief who comes “only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10). The hired hand who sees the wolf and runs (John 10:12).

Then he says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). David fought the lion and lived; a dead shepherd is no use to a flock. But Jesus does not say he will risk his life. He says he will lay it down, freely: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). His death is not the danger of the job. It is the job. The commentary on John 10 explores this verse by verse, and the study The Person & Work of Christ explains what it means that he died in our place.

Other sheep, one flock

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16). The fold was Israel. The other sheep are people from every nation. If you are not Jewish and you follow Jesus, you are one of those other sheep.

And once in his flock, they are safe. “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The study Assurance of Salvation, in its chapter The Promises of God: Anchors for the Doubting Soul, opens up this promise and the Father’s hand that holds the sheep as well.

On his shoulders, rejoicing

Luke gives us the same shepherd in a story. “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?” (Luke 15:4). The way to carry a frightened or exhausted sheep is still across the shoulders, its legs held together in front of the chest. Some of the earliest Christian art, in the Roman catacombs, shows exactly this.

But look at his face. “And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:5). No scolding, no sigh. He calls the neighbours to a party, and Jesus says heaven is like that over one sinner who repents. Many of us picture God receiving us back with a frown. Jesus pictures him rejoicing all the way home.

Struck, and raised

On the night of his arrest Jesus quoted Zechariah, “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26:31). The shepherd was struck by God’s own sword, bearing the judgment his wandering sheep deserved. “All we like sheep have gone astray … and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

But the struck shepherd did not stay down. Hebrews prays to “the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20). This shepherd died, rose, and is still shepherding. Peter calls him “the chief Shepherd” who will one day appear (1 Peter 5:4), and “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25).

The shepherd becomes the lamb

Here the picture turns over. Isaiah, in the same chapter that calls us straying sheep, describes the servant of the LORD “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent” (Isaiah 53:7). John the Baptist pointed at Jesus: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). The shepherd took the place of a sheep. He went where the lost lamb was going, to the slaughter, so that the lamb could come home.

And John’s vision of the redeemed in heaven puts both together. “For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17). The one on the throne of the universe is a Lamb, still bearing the marks of slaughter (Revelation 5:6). And the Lamb is the Shepherd. He knows what it is to be a sheep: he has been led, and silent, and slain, and on the cross he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). Nobody leads a flock to springs of water as tenderly as one who has himself been thirsty. The shepherd of the redeemed is the one who once lay down in their place. This is our God.

An example

A woman who had walked away from faith for twenty years came back to church after her mother’s funeral. She expected to feel like an outsider on probation. The sermon was on Luke 15, and she cried through most of it, because for the first time she pictured God not tolerating her return but rejoicing over it.

For reflection

What is the difference between a shepherd who risks his life and one who lays it down? How do you picture God receiving you when you come back after wandering? What does it mean to you that the one who shepherds his people for ever is the Lamb who was slain? Which picture in this chapter will you carry with you this week?

6.title: Living as His Sheep
6.essay:
If the Lord is our shepherd, then we are his sheep. That shapes how we listen, where we go, who we stay with, and how we face fear and even death. Everything here rests on what he has already done: he found us, carried us home, and laid down his life for us.

Listening to his voice

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). How do we hear him now? Not mainly in feelings or impressions, but in Scripture, where his voice is written down for us. The nearer a sheep stays to its shepherd, the better it knows his voice. So read the Bible, hear it preached, and let it become the voice you know best. Then you will be slower to follow the voices that only sound right.

Following

Eastern sheep followed the shepherd who went in front. Christ does not drive us from behind with threats. He goes ahead: into temptation, into suffering, into death, and out the other side. Following him is staying close to someone who has already walked the path. When the way ahead is unclear, the question is not “Can I see the whole road?” but “Can I see him?”

Staying with the flock

A sheep alone is a sheep in danger. Christians are not meant to follow Christ as solitary animals. He has “one flock” (John 10:16), and he places us in local churches. Drifting from the church usually happens as a sheep drifts: small steps, each easy, until we look up and find ourselves alone. Stay with the flock, even when it is awkward. The study The Church explores belonging further.

Under-shepherds

Christ shepherds his flock partly through people. Peter, writing to elders, says, “shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly … not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3). Paul tells the elders at Ephesus to watch “all the flock” because the church was bought with God’s own blood (Acts 20:28). This commentary holds that each local church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, with the congregation involved in key decisions, as the chapter Shepherds and Servants: Elders and Deacons in the study The Church explains. Elders are under-shepherds. The flock is not theirs. They answer to “the chief Shepherd” (1 Peter 5:4). Pray for them, and make their work a joy (Hebrews 13:17).

But some who call themselves shepherds behave like the thieves and hired hands of John 10. If a leader is abusing you, controlling, threatening, exploiting, or harming you or anyone else, your safety comes first. Get to safety. Tell someone you trust outside the situation. Where there is abuse of any kind, report it to the police or the proper authorities; a church’s own processes are never a substitute. Leaving such a place is not leaving Christ. The good Shepherd is angry at shepherds who harm his sheep (Ezekiel 34:10), and he binds up the injured.

Found when we wander

We will still wander. When you realise you have drifted, do not stay away out of shame. The Shepherd is already looking for you. Come back by the way all sheep come back: by turning to him, owning your sin, and trusting that he receives you with joy (Luke 15:5). The Shepherd who “restores my soul” (Psalm 23:3) does not run out of patience with his sheep.

Fear not, little flock

Sheep are anxious animals, and so are we. Jesus speaks to that directly. “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Little flock is a tender phrase. He does not pretend we are strong. He tells us the Father delights to give. When fear rises, tell him about it, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Anxiety is not always a spiritual failure. If it is overwhelming or will not lift, see a doctor; getting help, including medicine, is no failure of faith. The study Contentment & Anxiety has more on this.

The last valley

One valley every sheep must walk through is death. A psalm says of those who trust in their wealth, “Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd” (Psalm 49:14). That is the most frightening shepherd imaginable. But for Christ’s sheep, death is not the shepherd. It is only a valley, and the Shepherd walks it with them: “I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 23:4). He has already walked it himself, all the way to the bottom, and come up the other side.

That does not make grief small. We still weep when someone we love walks into that valley ahead of us, and the Shepherd weeps with us (John 11:35). But the sheep that goes through it goes home, “and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever” (Psalm 23:6). The study Death, Dying & Heaven explores this hope more fully.

An example

An elderly man in a hospice asked his daughter to read Psalm 23 every evening. Near the end he could no longer speak, but when she reached “for you are with me”, he would squeeze her hand. She says it was the clearest sermon she has ever heard.

For reflection

Whose voice do you hear most often during the week, and how could you hear the Shepherd’s voice more? Are you staying close to the flock, or drifting? How can you encourage and pray for the under-shepherds of your church? What fear do you need to hand to the Shepherd today, and how does Psalm 23:4 change the way you think about death?
